Text:
The velvet worm hunts with a glue gun, and the design is hundreds of millions of years old.

Two jets of sticky slime fire from nozzles near its head.

They reach prey up to a foot away and harden in seconds, trapping it in place.

The basic body plan has barely changed since, which makes it one of the closest things alive to a true living fossil.

What is the strangest hunting method you know of?

#velvetworm #invertebrates #wildlifefacts #livingfossil
Alt text(s): A velvet worm with a soft, ridged brown body and many stubby legs crawling over green moss, two fine slime threads trailing from the front of its head.
Comment(s): The slime jets fire from a pair of nozzles beside the head, and the velvet worm's body plan has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years, which is why it gets called a living fossil.

Text:
The yeti crab farms its own food on its arms.

Bacteria live in the dense, hair-like bristles covering its claws.

The crab combs them off with its mouthparts and eats them.

It waves its claws through the water to keep the crop alive, stirring fresh oxygen and chemicals past the bacteria.

Yeti crabs turn up at deep sea methane seeps and hydrothermal vents, where there is nothing else to eat.

#yeticrab #deepsea #oceanfacts #hydrothermalvent
Alt text(s): A pale yeti crab facing the camera on dark deep sea rock, its two claws covered in dense blond bristles, with bubbles rising in the black water behind it.
Comment(s): The bristles are the farm. The bacteria living in them are the crab's food supply, which is how an animal eats at a vent where nothing else grows.

Text:
Western hognose snake care, in six photos.

The cobra hood, the hissing, the mock strikes and playing dead with its tongue out: all bluff. Genuine aggression in this species is close to unheard of.

The setup is dry, with substrate deep enough to burrow in.

Hatchlings eat weekly, adults once every two weeks, because an adult fed weekly gets fat.

Respiratory infection comes from humidity running too high, so dampness is the thing to watch.

Given a choice in a 2022 study, the snakes picked the enriched side, and kept picking it.

Which bit of hognose theater have you seen in person?

#hognosesnake #westernhognose #snakecare #reptilekeeping
Alt text(s): A western hognose snake with its neck flattened into a defensive hood, the bluff display the caption describes.||A western hognose snake enclosure with deep loose substrate, a basking bulb overhead and hides at each end.||A western hognose snake taking a thawed mouse from feeding tongs inside a plain feeding container.||A western hognose snake being examined up close for signs of illness, its scales and upturned snout in view.||A western hognose snake burrowing nose first into loose substrate with its upturned snout.||A western hognose snake resting in a dry, deep-substrate enclosure.
Comment(s): The hognose's upturned snout is built for burrowing, which is why deep loose substrate and feeding away from that substrate both matter in a western hognose setup.

Text:
Hoatzin chicks hatch with two working claws on each wing, and they use them.

A chick knocked out of the nest can climb back up the branches hand over hand.

Or it drops into the river below to escape a predator, then hauls itself out.

The claws disappear as the bird matures.

Adults are nicknamed the stinkbird for a separate reason: they digest leaves by slow fermentation in an oversized crop, the same trick a cow's stomach uses, and a meal can take up to 45 hours to pass.

#hoatzin #birdfacts #amazonbirds #ornithology
Alt text(s): A hoatzin chick with wet, spiky brown down perched on a branch over brown river water, one wing raised to show the claws.
Comment(s): Hoatzin chicks keep the wing claws only while they need them, and the slow leaf fermentation in the adult's crop is the reason behind the stinkbird nickname.

Text:
Jumping spider care, in six photos, starting with the strangest fact.

A 2024 paper documents individual recognition in the regal jumping spider. It can tell spiders apart.

Handling: let it walk onto your hand, never grab it, always low over something soft. A fall can badly injure one.

The enclosure is small and vertical, about 8 inches tall, one spider each.

They eat live insects only, and the abdomen sets the schedule better than any calendar.

Dehydration is one of the most common reasons captive jumping spiders die, so humidity sits at 50 to 60 percent for the regal.

Would you keep a pet that recognizes you?

#jumpingspider #phidippusregius #regaljumpingspider #spidercare
Alt text(s): A regal jumping spider on a flat piece of cork bark, its large front eyes facing the camera.||A jumping spider walking onto an open hand during a calm, low handling session.||A small vertical jumping spider enclosure with coconut fiber substrate, climbing branches and a hygrometer.||A jumping spider eating a fruit fly on a leaf inside its enclosure.||A jumping spider with a plump abdomen resting near a misted enclosure wall.||A regal jumping spider perched near its small vertical enclosure and basic supplies.
Comment(s): Regal jumping spider eyesight is the reason handling works at all. It tracks your hand with those large forward-facing eyes and walks on when it decides to.
